div.head: Enclosure
div.p: The U.S. has decided to allay Israel’s concerns for its security and to seek an arms limitation in the Near East. Courses of action to avoid damage to U.S. fundamental interests in the area include adequate quid pro quo from Israel and demonstration of continued evenhandedness in overall U.S. policy in the area.

list.label: A.
list.item: To provide a greater degree of security assurance for Israel and its Arab neighbors vis-á-vis each other
list.label: B.
list.item: To secure an arms limitation in the Near East (Minimum: nuclear weapons and offensive missiles)
list.label: C.
list.item: To preserve fundamental interests of U.S. in area

p.hi: II. Fundamental U.S. Interests in Area

list.label: A.
list.item: Denial to Soviets
list.label: B.
list.item: Communications—commercial and strategic—access and transit; overflight; Suez Canal
list.label: C.
list.item: Petroleum—on which prosperity and economic strength U.K. and Western Europe depend
list.label: D.
list.item: Containment of Arab-Israel hostility
list.label: E.
list.item: Preventing proliferation nuclear weapons
list.label: F.
list.item: Reasonable degree of rapport with Arab world as well as with Israel

list.label: A.
list.item:
General 1.
Suspicious of U.S. intentions; however, evenhanded policy beginning produce results (greater willingness accommodate U.S. on difficult issues) 2.
Deep-seated resentment of Israel; however, more signs of passive acceptance Israel’s existence so long as issues not publicly agitated 3.
Fear of Israel’s military strength
a. Particularly nuclear weapons—if development appears imminent, UAR might feel obliged launch air attack
list.label: B.
list.item:
UAR Attitudes 1.
Egypt more prepared than other Arab states take long range view (often willing negotiate issues) so long as long range UAR interests advanced or at least not prejudiced 2.
Egyptians regard selves as natural leaders Arab world and obliged respond any threat Arab goals 3.
Desire cooperate with U.S. created by economic assistance and U.S. world leadership role; but must avoid appearing be tool of U.S. 4.
UAR considers that number of strains recently placed on US-UAR relations, viz: a.
Attacks on UAR in Congress and U.S. press b.
Declaration of direct or implied unilateral support and favor for Israel c.
UAR impatience at delays in fulfilling economic aid commitments d.
UAR claim that alarms over arms, Germans, and rockets exaggerated e.
U.S. military measures support Saudi Arabia and Jordan f.
Suspicion U.S. has hand in current frustration in Syria and Iraq
5.
Lack of confidence in constancy of U.S. policy toward UAR
6.
UAR readiness to deal with Soviets

list.label: A.
list.item:
Considers present moment most propitious for all-out campaign achieve principal foreign policy objectives 1.
U.S. Presidential election in 1964 2.
Psychological—impact German scientist and weapons charges against UAR; threat of Nasserist encirclement and call for Palestine liberation 3.
Military—confident of present military superiority 4.
Economic—large, fluid foreign exchange reserves and year or more of stocks food and other supplies
list.label: B.
list.item: Fears are for longer term potential of Arabs—however, Israeli public concerned by recent area developments—fears will be played up by government
list.label: C.
list.item: Determined maintain own freedom of action
list.label: D.
list.item: Believes Arab world can be depended on react unhelpfully to U.S. initiatives re area tensions
list.label: E.
list.item: Mistrustful of U.S. interests in Arab world and hopeful accomplish change in U.S. posture impartiality

p.hi: V. What Israel Seeks From the United States

list.item: Special, public guarantee of Israel’s security
Joint military planning and regular intelligence exchange
Access to U.S. weaponry (short of nuclears)
Discontinuance of U.S. support to the UAR
Demilitarization of West Bank of Jordan under UN in event of change of situation in Jordan
U.S. commitment to use military force to maintain status quo in Jordan
Public U.S. stand against Arab belligerency
Sustained high level of economic aid

item.p: U.S. support of “direct negotiations” resolution in UN; disavowal of UN resolutions on refugees; greater U.S. support for anti-Nasser forces in Near East; U.S. identification with and assistance to Israel’s aid programs, particularly in Africa; prevent Western participation in UAR weapons programs; USG support for special Israel ties with Europe.

p.hi: VI. Range of Possible Dangers to U.S. Interests From Security Assurance to Israel Alone—will depend on character U.S. approach, Israeli public posture, and possible Israeli concessions. US-Israel military coordination or change in arms policy would accentuate risks.

list.label: A.
list.item: Soviet counter-guarantee
list.label: B.
list.item: Public hostility throughout Arab world
list.label: C.
list.item: Consistent opposition U.S. initiative in UN and other bodies
list.label: D.
list.item: Weakening heretofore friendly regimes in Arab world—Lebanon, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait (incidentally, will tend rally Arabs around Nasser)
list.label: E.
list.item: Reduced U.S. diplomatic effectiveness generally, including circumscribed ability deal usefully with Arab-Israel issues (e.g. refugees, border violations, boycott, discrimination)
list.label: F.
list.item: Harassment oil companies and other U.S. commercial interests (nationalization not out of question)
list.label: G.
list.item: Closer Soviet-Arab military cooperation—in degree commensurate to alarm we may engender on part of Arabs (e.g., in extreme, we could not rule out Castro-type base arrangements)

div.p: VII. Quid pro Quos From Israel—required to protect U.S. interests in area

list.label: A.
list.item:
Minimum requirements during negotiations 1.
No publicity which will create problem for Nasser during negotiations 2.
Termination of campaign against U.S. policy, including aid to UAR 3.
Commitment of no movement of forces outside Israel (e.g., into West Bank) 4.
Cooperation in U.S. or IAEA inspections of nuclear installations
list.label: B.

item.p: Requirements in exchange for security assurance
[1 paragraph (1½ lines of source text) not declassified]

list.item: No territorial expansion
No cross-border military action
Cooperation with U.S. on UNTSO, refugee problem, Jordan waters

list.label: C.
list.item: Continuing Israel respect for international agreements previously entered into (e.g., General Armistice Agreement)

div.p: VIII. Steps—Essential that blanket of secrecy be put over entire operation at least through end June 1963

list.label: A.
list.item:
Presidential letter to Nasser (immediately) to note: 1.
Mounting pressure against U.S. policy aid to UAR 2.
Possible danger of preemptive attack by Israel 3.
Israel’s intent and capability develop nuclear weapons 4.
Set stage for Ambassador’s detailed discussions
list.label: B.
list.item:
Bearing in mind that success of current initiatives depends heavily on absolute secrecy at least of early steps, conduct campaign on Hill with view 1.
Quieting debate and agitation of Near East issues
2.
Achieving and maintaining necessary flexibility in aid program for UAR and other Arab states
list.label: C.
list.item: Initiate and continue parallel steps calculated preserve adequate negotiating atmosphere in UAR and minimize reaction in Arab states (See IX below)
list.label: D.
list.item: Approach to Israel Government to establish conditions for negotiation (see VII A above—utilize reply to Ben-Gurion’s May 14 letter to President)
list.label: E.
list.item: Ambassador (or special emissary) to initiate discussions in Cairo (with Nasser—early June) and Tel Aviv re arms limitation associated with security assurances to be offered both parties
list.label: F.
list.item: Receive and evaluate reactions; include follow-up discussions by ambassadors, particularly in Cairo, as necessary for clarifications (conclude by July 15)
list.label: G.
list.item: Second Round—discussions Cairo and Tel Aviv (July 15–30) beginning negotiations re arms limitation and related security assurances
list.label: H.
list.item: If no progress discernible in six months (by February 1964) through fault of UAR, revert to unilateral discussions with Israel for a security guarantee (timing must take into account status of Jordan Waters problem)
list.label: I.
list.item: If no progress on arms limitation discernible through fault of Israel after six months (assuming some progress with UAR) apply additional pressure on Israel
list.label: J.
list.item: By June 1964, have either a UAR-Israel arms limitation arrangement and security assurance or unilateral arms limitation and security assurance for Israel

p.hi: IX. Parallel Steps To Minimize Reaction in Arab States

list.item:
Be more responsive on economic assistance to UAR, taking initiative with UAR if necessary a.
Complete action on long pending commitments (e.g., ExIm and AID loans related Kaissouni mission) b.
Talk up possible consortium c.
Give some reassurance re possible development loans FY 64 (increase planning level)
Conclude Investment Guarantee Agreement and actively encourage American private investment moves to extent feasible (e.g., Sears Roebuck project)
Seek damping of Congressional attacks on UAR and U.S. policy
Maintain secrecy on contacts with Nasser
Public declaration by President of our good intentions toward the Arabs
Demonstrate continuation evenhanded policy on other aspects Arab-US-Israel relationship—e.g., in handling Jordan Waters issues and refugee problem
Continue refugee initiative—seek Israel cooperation
Maintain posture that we do not object to Arab Unity (subject to our criteria)
Seek damping of Congressional criticism Arab states and institutions
Avoid over-identification U.S. with Israel’s minor initiatives (e.g., Israel’s third country programs, ties with European regional organizations, etc.)
Continue special measures support Saudi Arabia and Jordan
Maintain and foster aid and other economic relations with Syria and Iraq
